solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mystery writer of 19th Century dictionary

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Wilkie ..., author of The Moonstone and The Woman in White
second meaning: the publisher founded in Glasgow in 1819, known for its dictionaries

explanation.surface: A crime novelist apparently penned a Victorian dictionary.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the Victorian sensation novelist and to the long-established publishing house behind a famous dictionary.

clue.text: Haddock for one likely eaten by noir writer

indicators.note: something eaten ends up inside whatever eats it, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: James M. Cain, author of The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity
apt to do something is likely to do it

explanation.surface: A haddock is probably going to be eaten by a hard-boiled crime novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Haddock looks like the fish, but it is Tintin's seafaring friend.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Haddock is the whisky-loving sea captain in Hergé's Tintin books, so he is one example of the rank.

clue.text: Plant books found in boozer, not hospital

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it, so one piece goes within the other
not tells us to take away the letter standing for the following word

parts.note: a lush is a heavy drinker
H is the abbreviation for hospital, as on road signs
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books

explanation.surface: Someone finds a stash of books in a pub, but no hospital nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: Boozer here is a drinker rather than the British slang for a pub; LUSH loses its H and then takes in OT.
explanation.definitionFit: The lotus is a water plant, sacred in several Asian religions, with large floating leaves and flowers.

clue.text: When one goes up to call a novice of Saint Clare

indicators.note: in a down entry something going up is read from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
the Roman numeral for one
to give someone a bell is British slang for phoning them
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone rises to summon a young nun of the Poor Clares.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the end, disguised as part of the story; it points to Shakespeare's Measure for Measure.
explanation.definitionFit: In Measure for Measure the heroine is about to enter the convent of the Poor Clares when her brother is condemned.

clue.text: Burma-born satirist mockingly ironic on radio

indicators.note: something heard on radio is heard and not seen, so we go by the sound of the word

parts.note: sarky is British slang for sarcastic, and in a non-rhotic accent the R is silent

explanation.surface: A satirist from Burma is broadcasting his sarcasm.
explanation.walkthrough: SARKY, the British colloquial form of sarcastic, sounds the same as the pen name in Southern British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki was the pen name of H. H. Munro, born in Akyab in Burma, famous for his barbed comic short stories.

clue.text: Play mother with cold and hot drinks option

indicators.note: whatever drinks something takes it inside, so the pair surrounds the next piece

parts.note: an informal word for mother
C marks the cold tap
your best bet is your best option
H marks the hot tap

explanation.surface: A mother at a café counter weighing cold drinks against hot ones.
explanation.walkthrough: Cold and hot are the letters on taps; read as a pair they swallow the option, rather than offering drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Scottish tragedy is named after its regicidal thane, so the title is a stage drama.

clue.text: Found recent mail relating to Antonio's work?

indicators.note: to found metal is to melt and cast it into a new shape, so these letters are recast

parts.note: taken as written: ten letters to be recast

explanation.surface: Someone has turned up some newly arrived letters to do with Antonio's job.
explanation.walkthrough: Found looks like the past tense of find, but it means cast. Antonio is the title character of The Merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio is Shakespeare's Venetian merchant, so anything about his trade concerns commerce and buying and selling.

clue.text: Persons known for seminal true crime book

definitions.text: Persons known for seminal true crime book
definitions.note: the plural reads as a general description; the answer is one writer's surname

parts.words: Persons known for seminal true crime book
parts.note: surface reading: an author celebrated for a groundbreaking non-fiction book about a real murder
setter's reading: the same French word is slang for a condom, the thing known for catching seed

explanation.surface: Writers famous for a landmark non-fiction book about a real crime.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cold Blood (1966), about a Kansas family's murder, pioneered the non-fiction novel; 'capote anglaise' is French slang for a condom, hence the joke in seminal.
explanation.definitionFit: Truman Capote wrote In Cold Blood, widely seen as the book that founded the modern true crime genre.

clue.text: Lie about with European Verne novel (in Dutch)

indicators.note: about means scattered around, so the letters of the words that follow are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
E is the standard abbreviation for European
taken as written: the French writer's surname

explanation.surface: Someone fibs about a Jules Verne book translated into Dutch.
explanation.walkthrough: Verne novel looks like it names the book, but novel belongs to the definition and Verne is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eline Vere (1889) is the first book by Louis Couperus, a Dutch writer, so it is a work of fiction in that language.

clue.text: Incentive to support fiery rebel

indicators.note: in a down entry a supporting piece sits underneath, so the first word comes below the second

parts.note: fiery means very hot
a spur is a goad or incentive

explanation.surface: An incentive to back a hot-headed insurgent.
explanation.walkthrough: Fiery rebel reads as one phrase, but fiery is wordplay and rebel alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Percy, nicknamed Hotspur, led an uprising against Henry IV and appears in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1.

clue.text: Way to befriend Afghan war author?

parts.note: a pat is a friendly way to approach a dog
an Afghan hound is a dog, and so a barker

explanation.surface: How do you make friends with an Afghan veteran writer?
explanation.walkthrough: Afghan suggests a war in Afghanistan beside war author, but it is the hound.
explanation.definitionFit: Pat Barker's Regeneration trilogy is set during the First World War, making her a celebrated novelist of that conflict.

clue.text: Publish Pinter plays with no end of menace

indicators.note: plays suggests the letters frolic about and end up rearranged
with no means a letter is removed from the word before

parts.note: taken as written: Harold Pinter's surname

indicators.note: end of picks out the final letter of the word that follows

parts.note: the final letter of menace

explanation.surface: Pinter's plays go to print without their famous comedy of menace.
explanation.walkthrough: Plays reads as a noun, Pinter's dramas, but it is the verb that jumbles his name.
explanation.definitionFit: To publish a text is to put it into type and issue copies, the everyday verb for producing books.

clue.text: Goethe play not opening gutted Estonian novelist

indicators.note: not opening tells us to drop the first letter of the title before it

parts.note: Faust is Goethe's two-part verse drama

indicators.note: gutted means emptied of insides, so only the outside letters survive

parts.note: the first and last letters of Estonian

explanation.surface: A Goethe drama fails to open, leaving an Estonian writer devastated.
explanation.walkthrough: Gutted, British slang for bitterly disappointed, here means hollowed out.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice and Emma, so she is one of the best-known English novelists.

clue.text: "Be scared, you – – that. But don't be afraid" (Faulkner)

definitions.text: "Be scared, you – – that. But don't be afraid" (Faulkner)

parts.words: "Be scared, you – – that. But don't be afraid"
parts.note: surface reading: a quotation from Faulkner with two words missing
setter's reading: the gap needs a phrase meaning you are unable to stop yourself

explanation.walkthrough: The two dashes mark a two-word gap; the line comes from Faulkner's advice that fear is natural but must not rule you.
explanation.definitionFit: Being scared is involuntary, so the missing phrase says it is beyond your control to avoid.

clue.text: What Mr. Peggotty might try and get for Scrooge?

definitions.text: What Mr. Peggotty might try and get
definitions.meaning: first meaning: Mr. Peggotty is the Yarmouth fisherman in David Copperfield, who would want a bargain flatfish
second meaning: Dickens's miser, whose name now means any tight-fisted person

explanation.surface: Wondering what one Dickens character might fetch for another.
explanation.walkthrough: Both names come from Dickens, inviting a plot connection, but one is a fisherman and the other a by-word for meanness.
explanation.definitionFit: A stingy person who hates spending is a skinflint or miser, and Scrooge is the classic example.

clue.text: Writer's lodge around cabin in New England

indicators.note: in tells us everything before goes inside the region named next

parts.note: NE is the usual abbreviation for New England

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to lodge somewhere is to live there
the S of the possessive ending
a cabin is a simple hut

explanation.surface: A writer's holiday lodge surrounds a cabin somewhere in New England.
explanation.walkthrough: New England is split open, its two letters bracketing everything else; the possessive ending supplies a letter of its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Nevil Shute was an English-born aeronautical engineer and novelist who wrote A Town Like Alice and On the Beach.

clue.text: It left vision blurred in one such as Holmes

indicators.note: a blurred image is out of focus and jumbled, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something leaves the sight of a great detective blurry.
explanation.walkthrough: Holmes suggests a detective, but the definition rests on his hobby, not his job.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherlock Holmes plays a Stradivarius to help himself think, so he is an example of a fiddle player.

clue.text: Briefly study purveyor of nonsense

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: to study something is to learn it

explanation.surface: A quick look at a dealer in drivel.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Lear wrote The Owl and the Pussy-cat and the Book of Nonsense, popularising limericks and comic verse.

clue.text: Nationality of Jane swinging with apes?

indicators.note: swinging means moving back and forth, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: What country is Jane from, swinging through the trees with Tarzan's apes?
explanation.walkthrough: Jane and the swinging apes call up Tarzan, which has nothing to do with the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being from Japan is a citizenship, and the adjective names that national identity.

clue.text: Club knocking vitality out of Elinor or Marianne?

indicators.note: knocking something out removes it, so one piece is taken away
out of names the larger word from which the piece is struck

parts.note: the sisters in Sense and Sensibility share this surname
dash means verve or vitality

explanation.surface: A club beating the life out of one of Austen's sisters.
explanation.walkthrough: Elinor and Marianne are the Dashwood sisters, heroines of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility.
explanation.definitionFit: In golf, a long-hitting club with a broad head was traditionally made of timber and still carries the name.

clue.text: No time to pardon right-on novelist

indicators.note: no says the following piece is missing from the next word

parts.note: pardon? and what? both ask someone to repeat themselves
RT is an abbreviation for right
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: There is no time to forgive a fashionably right-thinking writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Right-on, a sneer at fashionable liberal views, splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Wharton wrote The Age of Innocence and won the Pulitzer Prize, making her a noted American fiction writer.

clue.text: Father with revolutionary post in Urquhart's workplace

indicators.note: with and in together say the first word has the second inside it
in places the second piece within the first

parts.note: a father is a parent

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the following word is read backwards

parts.note: post is the British word for mail

explanation.surface: A father with a radical job at Urquhart's office.
explanation.walkthrough: Francis Urquhart is the scheming Chief Whip and Prime Minister in Michael Dobbs's House of Cards.
explanation.definitionFit: As a Conservative MP and then Prime Minister, Urquhart works in the Westminster legislature.

clue.text: Can heartless fantasist upset sickly lad?

parts.note: a can is a tin

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so in a down entry the letters run upwards
heartless means the centre letter is taken out

parts.note: Walter Mitty is Thurber's daydreamer, a by-word for a fantasist

explanation.surface: Can a callous dreamer distress a poorly boy?
explanation.walkthrough: Can looks like the verb opening a question, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny Tim is Bob Cratchit's crippled young son in A Christmas Carol, the classic ailing boy.

clue.text: Pen and the person using it, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a pen is an instrument that writes
second meaning: someone holding a pen is an author

explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a tool that makes marks on paper and an author who composes texts.

clue.text: A criminal pair, one case to suit Holmes?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: criminal means crooked, so the following word's letters are bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the next word count

parts.note: the first and last letters of suit

explanation.surface: Two crooks make a case worthy of Sherlock Holmes.
explanation.walkthrough: Criminal and case point to detection, but Holmes is defined by his retirement hobby.
explanation.definitionFit: In retirement Sherlock Holmes kept bees on the Sussex Downs, so he became a beekeeper.

clue.text: Amis makes first of terribly good notes here?

indicators.note: makes says one letter is made into another in the name

parts.note: Martin Amis, the novelist

indicators.note: first of picks out the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the opening letter of terribly
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Amis does terribly well where readers jot their comments.
explanation.walkthrough: Amis could be Kingsley or Martin; it is Martin whose T becomes G.
explanation.definitionFit: Readers scribble comments in the blank border beside the text, so that strip is where annotations go.

clue.text: Lime and the man who created him say

indicators.note: say means spoken aloud, so the sound of the name counts, not its spelling

parts.note: Graham Greene created Harry Lime, the racketeer of The Third Man

explanation.surface: A character called Lime and the author who invented him.
explanation.walkthrough: Lime looks like Harry Lime, which is why the man who created him makes sense; as the definition it is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Lime is a bright yellowish shade of the colour named for grass and leaves.

clue.text: Trouble having love for university poet and librarian

indicators.note: having one thing for another means a swap
for marks the letter that is replaced by the one before it

parts.note: fuss means bother or trouble
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A university poet who is also a librarian is getting into love trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Sam Walter Foss was an American versifier who worked as a public library director in Somerville, Massachusetts.

clue.text: I wasn't totally fed up with son-stealing idiot

indicators.note: someone stealing takes a thing into their keeping, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a twit is a fool
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A hungry child complains of a fool who kidnaps a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition speaks as the hungry orphan of Dickens who asked for more gruel.
explanation.definitionFit: Oliver famously wanted more food in the workhouse, so he is the boy who was still hungry.

clue.text: Ian's novel way of making up for mistakes

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Ian McEwan's 2001 novel about a lie and its consequences

definitions.text: way of making up for mistakes
definitions.meaning: second meaning: amends made for a wrong

explanation.surface: A fresh method of setting right one's errors.
explanation.walkthrough: Novel looks like the adjective meaning new, but it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's novel shares its title with the word for reparation or making amends for a sin or offence.

clue.text: Barrel about with maybe Holly or Hazel?

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the preceding word is read backwards

parts.note: a tun is a large cask
holly is an example of a tree, as maybe signals

explanation.surface: Two girls, Holly and Hazel, playing around a barrel.
explanation.walkthrough: Holly or Hazel looks like a pair of girls' names or one definition; Holly is wordplay and Hazel alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Hazel bears cobnuts and filberts, so it is a species of shrub or small tree grown for its kernels.

clue.text: "The mysterious magnet is either there, buried somewhere deep behind the –, or it is not" (Elizabeth Gilbert)

definitions.text: "The mysterious magnet is either there, buried somewhere deep behind the –, or it is not" (Elizabeth Gilbert)

parts.words: "The mysterious magnet is either there, buried somewhere deep behind the –, or it is not"
parts.note: surface reading: a quotation from Elizabeth Gilbert with a word missing
setter's reading: the gap needs the bone over the heart, behind which attraction is buried

explanation.walkthrough: The dash marks the gap; Gilbert, author of Eat Pray Love, is writing about attraction lodged in the chest.
explanation.definitionFit: Deep behind the flat bone in the middle of the chest lies the heart, where the magnet of attraction is buried.
